model_notes.cfa_comp1:
Comparing the unweighted ordinal versus ML
  • The ML version has better CFI, TLI, and SRMR in robust versions. Has worse RMSEA.
  • A non-robust CFI and TLI, which you can't really compare for the ordinal version, are better- way better than the ML version. It goes on to show that the robust stats heavily penalize for ordinality.
  • The unweighted ordinal version has slightly higher reliability omega than the ML version, at 0.89 versus 0.86.
  • Towing and comfort -- the weakest items -- have their R-square reduced from 47% to sub-40 from ordinal to ML.
Comparing unweighted versus weighted
  • Both ordinal and continuous robust CFI and TLI reduce by 0.3 to 0.5, which were already below the guideline value. The robust RMSEA likewise increases by 0.04 to 0.06, which is already horrible. The SRMR, on the other hand, worsens but remains decent before and after applying weight.
  • Applying a weight increase increases omega by 0.03 in ordinal and by 0.01 in ML.
  • Towing and comfort -- the weakest items -- improve in the R-square under the application of weight. In the original method, the effect is more profound.
model_notes.cfa_comp2:
Comparing the unweighted ordinal versus ML

  • Like the first model family, the unweighted. The ML version, compared to its unweighted ordinal sibling in the second family, has slightly better CFI, TLI, and SRMR, but, in robust versions, has a worse RMSEA.
  • Power perceptions have a slightly better unweighted ordinal omega than ML, but a slightly worse one for non-power.
  • Towing and comfort -- the weakest items -- have better R-squares compared to the first CFA across both ordinal and ML in this second CFA. And like the first CFA, the R-squared goes down in the ML version.

Comparing unweighted versus weighted

  • The robust CFI and TLI are just as bad in the weighted ordinal version as in the first CFÃ. The ML is much better in the weighted version.
Looking at the discriminant validity
  • The upper limit of Ronkko's confidence interval goes above 0.9 when weight is applied in either estimator. In fact in the ML version, it's as high as 0.97 and in both unweighted versions it's 0.86. Although model refit failed at 0.9, it's dangerously close.
model_notes.cfa_comp3:
The discriminant validity
Comparing the path loadings and stuff has become tedious, as in the other two model families. Here I'm going to look only at discriminant validity, which I feel should be the important criterion because, as I've noted in the modeling later, these two split constructs create a positive-definite problem.

This Comparison family 3 shows slightly lower discriminant validity between the two constructs than Comparison family 2 -- as I would have expected because this split of constructs was EFA-based, which wasn't super clean itself.

Across the four variants of (Continuous, ordinal) X (weighted, unweighted): the highest value of latent correlation can be seen in the ordinal weighted case of around 0.86, and the lowest value is in the continuous unweighted case of 0.78.

This creates some empirical support for using them separately. But I think the positive non-definite problem will still persist if two variables are highly correlated and don't really differ in their regression paths (or, in other words, the variable they're pointing to remains the same). However, it still might be useful to have them separately for the dominance analysis.

Of course, it is redundant to say, but Model family one doesn't have a discriminant validity problem because it has only one construct.
model_notes.U1a:
Range and comparable data show high latent correlations and the HTMT2 value is also near the guideline value where the problems start

This is the first time I've applied Ronkko's (2022) workflow -- they kind of criticized all the things I've done before to assess discriminant validity. And I've felt the problems along the way, too.

The numbers are not too legible here but these are the cases that would get flagged by his workflow of looking at the upper CI and comparing a chi^2 against a less restrictive model.

Although compatibility and range concerns may seem very similar, they are perhaps not similar enough to warrant a forced merge. From a theoretical standpoint, I still am going to merge them.

model_notes.B2.1.1b:
Model discussion:
Partial mediation model where the mediator is environmental benefits, the X variable is awareness of consequences, and we have two Y variables: attitude and injunctive norms
model_notes.B2.1.1d: B2.1.1B and B2.1.1D are essentially the same models, just structural paths repackaged as covariances.
model_notes.B2.1.1e:
B2.1a == B2.1.1b == B2.1.1d == B2.1.1e

The covariances are repackaged as a structural relationship.

This is an interesting excursion into how SEM really works and what happens underneath.
  • Leaving everything unchanged, just repackaging a covariance into a structural path has no effect on the downstream structural paths. For example everything that goes into intention remains unchanged.
  • Even the Symbolism ~ Attitude, AoC ~ Attitude, and BEnv ~ attitude paths remain the same.
  • Since injunctive norms now got a new arrow pointed towards it, the other arrows pointed towards it change in values. If I care about the magnitude of the structural paths of things explaining injunctive norms in this bigger model, in that case I need to be prudent about drawing other arrows as well.
  • And the interesting thing is that their ordering in strength also changed. The BEnv path dropped from 0.485 to 0.222 and the symbolism path dropped from 0.303 to 0.263. So the inclusion of ALC to injunctive norms matters for that ordering if we cared about that too.
  • The R-square of injunctive norms increases from 0.645 to 0.676 so I might ask myself: What is it that I'm gaining by drawing this arrow? What is it that I'm losing by replacing it with just a covariance term?
model_notes.B2.1a:
Model related discussion:
Interesting thing: if I don't allow the pink-ish covariance arrow between injunctive norms and attitude, the ORDINAL model fails to converge.

Warning message: lavaan->lav_step11_estoptim(): the optimizer (NLMINB) claimed the model converged, but not all elements of the gradient are (near) zero; the optimizer may not have found a local solution use check.gradient = FALSE to skip this check.

That, I think, is a bummer because I have introduced possible explanatory mechanisms for both attitude and injunctive norms in this model. That's not sufficient. Even after that the two variables still have unexplained correlated parts. Kind of beats the purpose of predictors.


The continuous version of the model, however, fits very nicely. Just like any continuous model compared to its ordinal counterpart, this continuous model seems to be doing very well in terms of the global fit statistics.


I'm going to show that in Model 2.1B.


Model 2.1 main hypothesis:

Awareness of consequences is a direct predictor of attitude

Model discussion:
Model 2.1B doesn't have the attitude-injunctive norm covariance pathway. It assumes that the upstream stuff adequately explains attitude and injunctive norm and the residual terms don't have any covariance. Whatever is observed is just noise.

This model didn't fit in the ordinal way. There was a convergence issue. The continuous one fit. Don't be fooled by its high global fit statistics -- it's a feature of the continuous estimator in general.

model_notes.B2.1b5:
Model discussion:
no exogenous variable has been allowed to covary with any endogenous variable, which has actually been the case for all models so far with auto.cov.y = F. In other models, I explicitly had to allow the exogenous variables to covary with some endogenous variables. Here I haven't done so.

Here you see the negative variance problem again.

The lesson is that when you claim that you are fully explaining your endogenous variable with some predictors, it clearly covaries strongly independently -- it might lead to incorrect specification and counterintuitive results.

In this model symbolism and environmental benefits both have significant loadings on injunctive norms but one of them is negative and the other one is positive.
model_notes.B2.2.1a:
Global fit statistics are better in this expanded model with the dispositional account (B2.2.1A) compared to B2.1.1D.

  • Direct effects of both norms on intention became insignificant compared to 2.1.1D. Also, injunctive norm flips in its sign. Note that we allowed both norms to freely covary with these new variables.
  • Direct effects of AoC on attitude become insignificant and flip in sign compared to 2.1.1D. The total effect of AoC on attitude decreases in magnitude but remains significant.

  • The direct effect of AoC on attitude is negative and non-significant. That inflates the indirect effect of AoC on attitude -- this is the reason I'm going to remove the path and see what happens in Model 2.2.3C.

model_notes.B3.1a:
In this first utility-addition step, I am adding only the clean, reflective variables.

  • Attitude ~ Observability regression coefficient is negative (counterintuitive) and significant.
  • Their original latent correlation was 0.42713 (see CFA of utility account, any model, U2B)
  • Descriptive norms had a knack for often breaking in the past in the sense that it shows a negative sign and insignificance. Same thing happening here.
  • The rest of the results have intuitive signs and all are significant.
model_notes.B3.1b1:
Issues I faced
  • Empirically, I don't have the robust CFI and TLI to keep comparing.
  • Next, I tried fitting these variables as formative latent variables with their own disturbance terms, but in an ordinal setting, it was impossible with different settings. Among other things, I tried scaling the causal indicators, emitting two or more paths from the reflective variable, and scaling one of those paths (for example, the performance perception-to-attitude path) to 1. All attempts failed. The model never converged or was never identifiable.
  • The ML approach succeeded.
Results
  • Comparing with model 3.1, injunctive norm --> intention becomes negative (counterintuitive) but remains significant, while descriptive norm --> intention becomes significant and becomes positive (intuitive).
  • Observability --> attitude becomes insignificant. Perhaps due to the addition of other variables that are correlated with observability. Some sort of suppression effect
  • Other comparable things retain the same sign and significance.
model_notes.B3.1c:
• SRMR and robust RMSEA become better. Robust CFI and robust TLI get slightly worse.

model_notes.B3.1c3:
Warning messages: 1: lavaan->lav_data_full(): 12 cases were deleted due to missing values in exogenous variable(s), while fixed.x = TRUE. 2: lavaan->lav_object_post_check(): some estimated ov variances are negative
Comparing the model B3.1C3 with its own ML version
What changes from ordinal to ML?
  • In the ordinal version, both norms were significant, and the injunctive norm had a counterintuitive sign. In the ML version, the descriptive norm becomes negative in a counterintuitive way, but it also becomes insignificant.
  • Observability on attitude flips in sign and gets positive (from a counterintuitive negative).
  • The trialability composite on attitude goes from -0.2 to +0.1 and remains significant.
  • Public charger access --> Attitude almost becomes insignificant at 4%.
What doesn't change but remains interesting?
  • Power perception --> Attitude remains counterintuitively negative and significant.
  • Non-power perception increases in magnitude and remains significant.
  • Non-power perception seems to be stealing some influence from power perceptions.
  • The cost composite reduces almost 10-fold and becomes almost insignificant.
  • R-square of intention drops from 83% to 75% in the ML version. PBC, attitude, and norms all see some sort of drop in their R-square as well.
The ML model has visibly worse CFI and TLI and SRMR compared to the robust version but has better RMSEA. And all those tabs are independently failing the guideline.

Worth noting that I don't have the robust versions for the ordinal model because it was not positive definite and typically I compare the robust stats for ordinal. A comparison of non-robust wouldn't be too appropriate.

I assume from similar trends that the gap in robust stats would be less between the two types of models.

Interesting. The only way this model differed from Model B3.1C2 is that I didn't allow any path from non-power perceptions to PBC. This reduces the impact of power perception on PBC, and that path also becomes insignificant.

Most importantly, this model, like the previous one, exhibits a non-positive-definite structure. The lowest eigenvalue is slightly negative, as I found after some digging with ChatGPT. Further digging showed a linear combination in the problematic eigenvalue direction and the problem might be associated with descriptive and injunctive norm so I'm going to merge them. And see what happens. Hopefully the positive definite problem will go away.
